> You’ve crossed the “hobby” threshold. You boot reliably, emit real metrics, and have a runner that parses/exports results.
  That’s a foundation for a research OS. The big question now is “what will make this distinctly AI‑native and publishable?”
  Below are major paths, each with what it is, why it matters, and where it leads.
  
  North Star
  
  - Build an AI‑native OS that treats models, dataflow, and latency SLOs as first‑class, with strong isolation, observability,
  and deterministic behavior.
  
  Path 1: Deterministic, Real‑Time AI OS
  
  - What: Make inference and small training loops predictable and repeatable. Think “same inputs → same outputs → within the
  same time budget.”
  - Why: Determinism and latency guarantees are rare in hobby kernels; they unlock robotics, audio/vision pipelines, and
  safety‑critical demos.
  - Leads To: Real‑time AI workloads (robot control loops, embedded vision), low‑latency edge inference that can be
  benchmarked and compared.
  - First Milestones:
      - Lock timing sources; stabilize tick/cycle accounting; remove nondeterministic kernel paths.
      - Deterministic scheduler mode with deadlines and admission control.
      - “Deterministic Inference” demo: fixed graph, fixed weights, fixed inputs → reproducible latency histogram and outputs.
  - Success Metrics:
      - Jitter P99 under target (e.g., inference frame P99 < X ms).
      - Reproducibility across boots (output hash and latency distribution stable).
  
  Path 2: Dataflow‑First Kernel (Graph‑Native Compute)
  
  - What: Treat the whole system as a graph of operators (nodes) passing tensors/messages (edges). The kernel schedules the
  graph, not just threads.
  - Why: AI workloads are graphs; making this the kernel’s “native object model” simplifies zero‑copy, co‑scheduling, and
  SLO enforcement.
  - Leads To: Fast pipelines, clean composition of models, clear places to attach QoS and isolation, and publishable “graph
  OS” results.
  - First Milestones:
      - Kernel object types: Port, Channel, Operator; zero‑copy shared memory for tensor objects with versioning.
      - Simple graph scheduler: topology‑aware, respects per‑edge latency budgets.
      - “Graph as a File” or syscall API: load/run/update graphs at runtime.
  - Success Metrics:
      - End‑to‑end graph latency improvement vs. process model.
      - Copy‑elimination counts and cache friendliness (PMU counters).
  
  Path 3: Model‑ and Privacy‑First Security
  
  - What: Models are first‑class citizens with capabilities: who may load, run, inspect, or export activations/gradients. Add
  attestation and sealed storage.
  - Why: Makes the project relevant for privacy‑sensitive AI (health, finance). Distinguishes you from “generic” microkernels.
  - Leads To: Trusted inference/training on edge nodes; potential TEE integration later; publishable work on “model as a
  principal.”
  - First Milestones:
      - Capabilities for “Model” objects (load/run/read/inspect).
      - Signed model packages with measured load and runtime audit trail.
      - Encrypted, versioned model store with rollback protection.
  - Success Metrics:
      - Complete audit of model lifecycle events.
      - Policy enforcement proven with unit/integration tests and formal specs for core capability checks.
  
  Path 4: Single‑System‑Image for AI Clusters (Microkernel Across Nodes)
  
  - What: A minimal, fast transport + RPC + scheduler that makes multiple QEMU instances feel like one “AI computer.”
  - Why: Distributed AI is the norm. Even a small, clean single‑system‑image (SSI) for graphs would be a standout
  contribution.
  - Leads To: Scaling demos (pipeline parallelism, model sharding), byzantine tests with real transport, and publishable
  distributed systems results.
  - First Milestones:
      - Low‑latency message fabric (shared‑memory on one host; sockets/virtio‑net across QEMU) with backpressure.
      - Cluster scheduler that places operators across nodes with data locality.
      - Replicated control plane with simple consensus only where needed (not the data path).
  - Success Metrics:
      - Throughput/latency scaling for multi‑node graphs.
      - Stable failover behavior for control plane (tested via fault injection).
  
  Path 5: Observability, Proof, and Safety
  
  - What: End‑to‑end tracing for AI pipelines plus targeted formal checks on critical code (alloc, scheduling, capabilities).
  - Why: Research credibility. Traces make results reproducible; formal specs make claims defensible.
  - Leads To: Papers and posts with time‑aligned traces, perf counters, and machine‑checkable properties.
  - First Milestones:
      - Stable in‑kernel tracepoints for graph events; export to JSON; replay tooling.
      - Property tests and lightweight model checking for the scheduler/capabilities.
      - PMU integration: consistent counters and attribution to operators.
  - Success Metrics:
      - Replay reproduces latency profiles within tolerance.
      - Safety properties (no leaks, no capability escalation) hold under fuzz and proofs.
  
  Path 6: Heterogeneous Acceleration Envelope (Optional, Parallel Track)
  
  - What: A clean HAL for CPU/NEON/NPU/GPU with a common “tensor op” surface and fallback emulation.
  - Why: When you touch real hardware, you’ll be ready. Even under QEMU, a good HAL plus emulation is publishable.
  - Leads To: Easy uplifts to real boards; credible comparisons of backends; future NPU enablement.
  - First Milestones:
      - Define tensor op ABI (allocate, map, run, sync) with strict lifetimes.
      - Emulated NPU device with the same ABI; run the same graph on CPU/NEON/emulated NPU.
      - Queueing and scheduling policies per accelerator class.
  - Success Metrics:
      - Zero code changes to switch backends for a graph.
      - Clear wins from specialization (cycles/byte, energy hints when possible).
  
  Recommended Route (Pragmatic)
  
  - Phase 1 (4–6 weeks): Dataflow‑First + Observability
      - Ship kernel‑level graph objects, zero‑copy channels, and a simple graph scheduler.
      - Add tracepoints and PMU counters tied to operator execution.
      - Deliverable: “Graph OS” demo with end‑to‑end latency improvement and clean traces.
  - Phase 2 (6–8 weeks): Deterministic Mode + Model Capabilities
      - Deterministic scheduler mode with deadlines/admission control.
      - Model capability system and signed model loading with an audit trail.
      - Deliverable: Deterministic inference demo; policy tests proving model isolation.
  - Phase 3 (8–10 weeks): Multi‑Node SSI Prototype
      - Minimal RPC fabric, node discovery, and graph placement across two QEMU nodes.
      - Deliverable: Throughput scaling demo; fault injection showing graceful degradation.
  
  Why this mix works
  
  - It stays true to “AI‑native” (graphs/models first), not a generic microkernel.
  - It yields measurable, publishable results at each step (latency reduction, determinism, isolation, scaling).
  - It sets clean interfaces for later hardware acceleration without blocking on hardware today.
  
  How you’ll know you’re “research‑grade”
  
  - You can load a graph, trace its execution, prove its policies, reproduce its timing, and scale it across nodes — all with
  clear, minimal interfaces.
  - Your benchmarks show improvements over process/thread baselines and over naive distributed runs.
  - Your docs let others reproduce results on QEMU and (optionally) dev boards.
  
  If you want, I can draft a short DESIGN.md for the “Graph OS” kernel objects and scheduler, plus a 6‑week milestone
  breakdown with testable endpoints.

> Below is a Claude-facing consultation request and operating protocol adapted from your Multi‑AI protocol, but tailored for
  the AI‑native kernel. It positions Claude as the primary technical advisor (architecture, implementation best practices, and
  research synthesis), and asks for industry‑grade guidance plus up‑to‑date references to drive concrete next decisions.
  
  Consultation Protocol (Kernel Adaptation)
  
  - Role: Claude acts as Principal Technical Advisor for an AI‑native kernel: architecture, scheduling, memory, isolation,
  dataflow, observability, determinism, and distributed execution.
  - Scope: A no_std AArch64 kernel that boots on QEMU UEFI, emits real METRICs, has a test runner, and targets AI‑native
  primitives (graphs/models/dataflow/latency SLOs), not a generic hobby OS.
  
  Consultation Request Template (for Claude)
  
  CONSULTATION REQUEST: Claude
  DOMAIN: Architecture, Implementation, Optimization, Research Synthesis
  CONTEXT:
  
  - Project: SIS AI‑Native Kernel. Boots on AArch64 QEMU via UEFI; brings up UART, MMU, heap, GICv3, PMU; emits METRICs
  (real_ctx_switch_ns, irq_latency_ns, ai_inference_us, etc.). Test runner parses metrics, exports JSON, and applies
  QEMU‑aware thresholds. Codebase uses Rust nightly, no_std, custom heap, minimal drivers, and has a “strict” lint gate for
  CI.
  - Vision: AI‑native OS where models, tensors, and dataflow graphs are first‑class; low‑jitter, deterministic execution;
  security modeled around models and data; scalable to multi‑node single‑system‑image (SSI) for AI graphs.
  - Near‑term targets:
      - Dataflow‑first kernel objects (Operator/Port/Channel/Tensor) with zero‑copy and backpressure.
      - Deterministic scheduler mode with deadlines/admission control for inference loops.
      - Model‑centric security (capabilities, signed model packages, attestation hooks).
      - Observability via structured tracing aligned to operators and tensors, plus PMU/cycle attribution.
      - Multi‑node SSI prototype (minimal RPC fabric and graph placement).
  PROBLEM:
  - We need an industry‑grade blueprint and best practices to evolve from a solid bring‑up + metrics kernel to a
  research‑credible AI‑native OS.
  - We want concrete, staged implementation plans that balance kernel minimalism with AI‑specific features, with measurable
  milestones and CI‑friendly validation.
  CONSTRAINTS:
  - Rust no_std, AArch64 focus; QEMU primary for now (hardware optional later).
  - Keep kernel surface minimal; prefer capability‑based isolation, zero‑copy paths, and deterministic behavior where
  possible.
  - Maintain parseable METRICs and JSON outputs for CI and reproducibility.
  EXPECTED OUTPUT:
  - Best practices and reference designs for:
      - Dataflow‑native kernel primitives (graph/scheduler/zero‑copy/shared memory/backpressure).
      - Deterministic scheduling for AI loops (deadline/EDF variants, admission control, timer discipline).
      - Model‑centric security (capabilities, signed models, secure model store, measurement/attestation path).
      - Observability (tracepoints, PMU integration, end‑to‑end flow tracing, replayability).
      - Multi‑node SSI (transport, placement, minimal consensus for control plane).
  - A staged technical roadmap (12–20 weeks) with crisp milestones, validation criteria, and CI hooks.
  - Up‑to‑date research and industry references (papers, systems, standards) linked to each topic, with 1–2 sentence
  annotations on relevance and what to borrow.
  INTEGRATION:
  - Each recommendation should include:
      - Minimal kernel API surface (syscalls or in‑kernel object interfaces).

▌Here is the comprehensive architectural plan for the SIS AI-Native Kernel.
▌
▌## Executive Blueprint: An AI-Native, Dataflow-First Kernel
▌
▌The SIS Kernel's vision is to treat AI/ML workloads not as applications *on* an OS, but as the fundamental organizing
▌principle *of* the OS. Traditional kernels schedule threads; the SIS kernel schedules **dataflow graphs**. Traditional
▌kernels manage memory pages; SIS manages **tensors**. This shift allows for unprecedented performance, security, and
▌determinism for AI workloads.
▌
▌Our architecture is founded on three key choices:
▌
▌1.  **Dataflow as the Core Abstraction**: We abandon the POSIX model of processes and threads. The only unit of execution is
▌an **Operator** within a static **Graph**. Data flows between operators via bounded **Channels**. This model naturally
▌provides backpressure, eliminates entire classes of concurrency bugs, and makes system behavior analyzable.
▌2.  **Capabilities as the Unified Security Primitive**: There are no users, groups, or ACLs. There are only **Capabilities**—
▌unforgeable tokens granting specific rights to specific kernel objects (a graph, a tensor, a model). This fine-grained,
▌model-centric approach provides strong isolation and adheres to the principle of least privilege.
▌3.  **Measurability as a Prerequisite**: Every architectural component is designed from day one to be observable. The kernel
▌emits high-fidelity `METRIC` tracepoints for every significant event, enabling precise performance analysis, determinism
▌validation, and robust CI.
▌
▌This plan executes this vision over a 16-week period, transforming the current proof-of-concept into a single-system-image
▌(SSI) prototype ready for enterprise and research evaluation.
▌
▌### High-Level Roadmap (16 Weeks)
▌
▌| Weeks   | Phase                               | Key Deliverables & Milestones
▌|
▌| :------ | :----------------------------------
▌| :--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
▌-------------------------------------------------------------- |
▌| **1-6** | **Phase 1: Dataflow & Observability** | • Kernel Object Model (`Graph`, `Operator`, `Tensor`, `Channel`)
▌implemented.\<br\>• Static, priority-based dataflow scheduler operational.\<br\>• Core observability tracepoints (`op_run`,
▌`channel_enqueue`) integrated.\<br\>• **Milestone:** A multi-operator graph (e.g., Sobel filter) runs correctly and exports
▌performance `METRIC`s to CI. |
▌| **7-12**| **Phase 2: Determinism & Security** | • Deterministic (EDF) scheduler mode implemented with admission control.
▌\<br\>• `Model` object with package signing and measurement.\<br\>• Capability system for model loading and execution.\<br\>•
▌**Milestone:** A real-time graph executes with verifiable jitter bounds (\<1µs), and a request to load an unsigned `Model` is
▌correctly rejected. |
▌| **13-16**| **Phase 3: Multi-Node SSI** | • Network-transparent `RemoteChannel` implemented.\<br\>• Node discovery and
▌simple graph placement heuristics.\<br\>• Control plane with minimal Raft consensus for placement decisions.\<br\>•
▌**Milestone:** A single graph is transparently partitioned and executed across two QEMU nodes, with backpressure correctly
▌propagating across the network link. |
▌
▌-----
▌
▌## Phase 1: Dataflow-First + Observability (Weeks 1-6)
▌
▌**Goal:** Establish the core dataflow execution model and prove its correctness and measurability.
▌
▌### Architecture: Kernel Object Model
▌
▌The kernel will manage a minimal set of first-class objects. All objects are created via system calls that return a
▌`Capability` handle.
▌
▌  * **`Graph`**: The unit of resource isolation and scheduling context. Owns `Operator`s and `Channel`s. Lifecycle: `Create`
▌-\> `Ready` (operators/channels added) -\> `Running` -\> `Destroyed`.
▌  * **`Operator`**: A non-preemptible unit of computation. Contains a code pointer and input/output **`Port`s**. It does not
▌own state; all state is passed via `Tensor`s.
▌  * **`Channel`**: A bounded, single-producer, single-consumer (SPSC) queue that transports `Tensor` handles. It is the sole
▌mechanism for data transfer and synchronization between `Operator`s.
▌  * **`Tensor`**: A handle to a physically contiguous memory region with metadata (shape, type, version). Tensors are
▌versioned to enable zero-copy "snapshot" semantics between operators. Ownership is transferred upon enqueue/dequeue.
▌  * **`Capability`**: An unforgeable `u64` token representing a right (e.g., `WRITE` on a `Channel`, `RUN` on a `Graph`). The
▌kernel maintains a capability table mapping these tokens to objects and rights.
▌
▌<!-- end list -->
▌
▌```plantuml
▌@startuml
▌hide empty members
▌skinparam classAttributeIconSize 0
▌
▌class Graph {
▌  id: u64
▌}
▌
▌class Operator {
▌  id: u64
▌  fn_ptr: *const ()
▌}
▌
▌class Channel {
▌  id: u64
▌  capacity: usize
▌}
▌
▌class Tensor {
▌  id: u64
▌  phys_addr: usize
▌  metadata: TensorMetadata
▌  version: u32
▌}
▌
▌class Port {
▌  direction: In/Out
▌}
▌
▌Graph "1" *-- "N" Operator
▌Graph "1" *-- "N" Channel
▌Operator "1" *-- "N" Port
▌Port "1" -- "1" Channel
▌@enduml
▌```
▌
▌### Scheduling and Dataflow
▌
▌The Phase 1 scheduler is a simple, non-preemptive, priority-based dataflow scheduler.
▌
▌  * **Execution Loop**: The scheduler iterates through all `Runnable` `Operator`s in a `Graph` (i.e., those with data
▌available on all input `Port`s). It executes the one with the highest static priority.
▌  * **Backpressure**: When an `Operator` attempts to enqueue a `Tensor` to a full `Channel`, the `Operator`'s execution
▌completes, but it is marked as `BlockedOnOutput`. It will not become `Runnable` again until space is available. This is the
▌fundamental flow-control mechanism.
▌  * **Co-scheduling**: Not implemented in Phase 1. All operators are scheduled independently.
▌
▌### Sequence Diagram: Graph Execution Cycle
▌
▌```plantuml
▌@startuml
▌participant Scheduler
▌participant OperatorA
▌participant ChannelAB
▌participant OperatorB
▌
▌Scheduler ->> OperatorA: activate()
▌activate OperatorA
▌OperatorA ->> OperatorA: process(input_tensors)
▌OperatorA ->> ChannelAB: enqueue(output_tensor)
▌activate ChannelAB
▌ChannelAB-->>OperatorA: success
▌deactivate ChannelAB
▌OperatorA-->>Scheduler: yield()
▌deactivate OperatorA
▌
▌Scheduler ->> Scheduler: find_runnable_ops()
▌note right: OperatorB is now runnable
▌
▌Scheduler ->> OperatorB: activate()
▌activate OperatorB
▌OperatorB ->> ChannelAB: dequeue()
▌activate ChannelAB
▌ChannelAB-->>OperatorB: output_tensor
▌deactivate ChannelAB
▌OperatorB ->> OperatorB: process(output_tensor)
▌OperatorB-->>Scheduler: yield()
▌deactivate OperatorB
▌@enduml
▌```
▌
▌-----
▌
▌## Phase 2: Deterministic Mode + Model Capabilities (Weeks 7-12)
▌
▌**Goal:** Provide hard real-time guarantees for AI loops and implement a secure, model-centric capability system.
▌
▌### Architecture & Scheduling
▌
▌This phase introduces a new, distinct scheduling mode. A `Graph` must be created as either `BestEffort` (using the P1
▌scheduler) or `Deterministic`.
▌
▌  * **Deterministic Scheduler**: We'll implement a **fixed-priority or Earliest Deadline First (EDF)** scheduler.
▌      * **Admission Control**: When a `Deterministic` graph is loaded, the user must specify its workload parameters (e.g.,
▌Worst-Case Execution Time (WCET), period, deadline). The kernel's scheduler performs an admission control test. If it cannot
▌mathematically guarantee that this new graph and all existing deterministic graphs will meet their deadlines, the load
▌request is rejected.
▌      * **Timer Discipline**: The kernel will rely on the ARM architected timer to drive scheduling ticks. All deterministic
▌execution occurs within these ticks.
▌      * **Invariants**: To preserve determinism, an `Operator` running in this mode is forbidden from performing any action
▌that could block indefinitely or have variable latency. This includes no dynamic memory allocation, no unbounded loops, and
▌no spinning. These constraints must be enforced.
▌
▌### Security Architecture
▌
▌Security is centered on the new **`Model`** kernel object. A `Model` is an immutable, signed package containing a
▌pre-compiled `Graph` and its associated weights.
▌
▌  * **Model-Centric Capabilities**:
▌      * **`LOAD_MODEL`**: A system-wide capability required to request the loading of a new model from a memory buffer.
▌      * **`RUN_MODEL`**: A capability returned after a successful, *measured* load. This token is tied to the specific hash
▌of the loaded model.
▌  * **Secure Loading Process**:
▌    1.  User-space requests to load a model package, providing the `LOAD_MODEL` capability.
▌    2.  The kernel receives the model package (e.g., in a shared buffer).
▌    3.  The kernel **measures** the package by computing its SHA-256 hash.
▌    4.  The kernel verifies the package's digital signature against a pre-loaded public key.
▌    5.  If both checks pass, the kernel creates the `Model` object and returns a `RUN_MODEL` capability to the user. This
▌capability is internally associated with the measurement hash.
▌  * **Secure Model Store**: While the full store is a user-space concern, the kernel provides the primitives. The kernel will
▌only load models from physically contiguous memory regions passed by a trusted user-space manager, which is responsible for
▌decryption and version management.
▌
▌-----
▌
▌## Phase 3: Multi-Node SSI Prototype (Weeks 13-16)
▌
▌**Goal:** Create a two-node prototype that can transparently execute a single `Graph` across a network boundary.
▌
▌### Architecture and Dataflow
▌
▌The key abstraction is making inter-node communication look like a local `Channel`.
▌
▌  * **`RemoteChannel`**: This kernel object presents the same SPSC queue interface as a local `Channel`. Internally, however,
▌its `enqueue` operation serializes the `Tensor` handle and metadata, and sends it over the network (VirtIO-net in QEMU) to
▌the peer node.
▌  * **Placement Heuristics**: The initial placement strategy will be manual. A privileged user-space process will define the
▌graph and explicitly assign each `Operator` to a specific node (`Node 0` or `Node 1`). The kernel will enforce this
▌placement, automatically inserting `RemoteChannel`s where the graph topology crosses the node boundary.
▌  * **Consensus (Minimalism is Key)**:
▌      * **Data Plane**: **No consensus.** Data flow is managed entirely by the inherent backpressure of the (now networked)
▌channels.
▌      * **Control Plane**: A minimal **Raft** implementation will be used *only* for managing cluster membership and agreeing
▌on graph placement decisions. It is not involved in the execution of the graph itself. This keeps the low-latency data path
▌free of consensus overhead.
▌  * **Fault Tolerance**: The P3 prototype's strategy is simple: if a node fails, any graph with operators placed on that node
▌is considered failed and terminated. A user-space orchestrator is responsible for restarting it.
▌
▌-----
▌
▌## Cross-Cutting Concerns
▌
▌### Observability
▌
▌The existing `METRIC` system will be extended. CI must track these metrics and fail builds on regression.
▌
▌  * **Phase 1**: `op_latency_p50_ns`, `op_latency_p99_ns`, `channel_depth_max`, `scheduler_run_us`, `zero_copy_count`.
▌  * **Phase 2**: `deterministic_deadline_miss_count`, `deterministic_jitter_ns`, `model_load_success_count`,
▌`model_load_auth_fail_count`.
▌  * **Phase 3**: `remote_channel_latency_p99_us`, `consensus_commit_latency_ms`.
▌  * **PMU Attribution**: The scheduler will be responsible for programming the AArch64 PMU (Performance Monitoring Unit)
▌before activating an `Operator` and reading the results after. This allows us to attribute events like cache misses and
▌branch mispredictions directly to specific operators.
▌
▌### Validation and CI Hooks
▌
▌  * **JSON Schemas**: A stable JSON schema for the `METRIC` output will be defined in a shared repository and used by the
▌test runner to validate output before analysis.
▌  * **QEMU vs. Hardware**: The CI will initially use generous thresholds based on QEMU's performance. A separate
▌configuration file will define much stricter thresholds for optional hardware runs. A key metric will be the
▌`qemu_hw_perf_ratio` to track how closely the emulation matches reality.
▌
▌### Risk Register
▌
▌| Phase | Risk                                                    | Mitigation
▌|
▌| :---- | :------------------------------------------------------
▌| :--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
▌--------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
▌| **P1** | **Dataflow performance is poor due to scheduler overhead.** | The initial scheduler is intentionally simple. Focus
▌on correctness first. The detailed observability metrics will pinpoint exactly where time is spent, guiding P2 optimizations.
▌|
▌| **P2** | **Achieving sub-microsecond determinism is extremely difficult.** | Isolate the deterministic scheduler and its
▌operators aggressively. Start with a trivial "hello world" deterministic graph. Use formal methods (inspired by seL4) to
▌reason about timing invariants. |
▌| **P3** | **Network overhead makes SSI unusable.** | Focus obsessively on zero-copy on the wire. The `RemoteChannel` should
▌transfer ownership of the `Tensor` handle, with the data buffer itself being sent via a highly optimized transport. Batch
▌small messages. |
▌
▌-----
▌
▌## References & Actionable Takeaways
▌
▌1.  **seL4: Formal Verification of an OS Kernel** (2009, SOSP)
▌
▌      * **Annotation**: The landmark paper on creating a mathematically proven secure microkernel. Its core ideas are a
▌minimal kernel surface and capability-based security.
▌      * **Takeaways**:
▌          * Adopt a minimal kernel object model; push complex policy into user-space.
▌          * Implement capabilities as the fundamental primitive for all access control.
▌          * Strive for a small, formally analyzable Trusted Computing Base (TCB).
▌
▌2.  **The Art of Multiprocessor Programming** (Book, Herlihy & Shavit)
▌
▌      * **Annotation**: The definitive guide to concurrent data structures, including lock-free queues.
▌      * **Takeaways**:
▌          * Implement the `Channel` object using a bounded, lock-free SPSC queue for maximum performance and to avoid
▌priority inversion in the deterministic scheduler.
▌          * Use memory ordering primitives (`acquire`/`release`) correctly to ensure visibility without expensive locks.
▌
▌3.  **Dapper, a Large-Scale Distributed Systems Tracing Infrastructure** (2010, Google Research)
▌
▌      * **Annotation**: The paper that introduced modern distributed tracing. Its principles are low overhead,
▌application-level transparency, and scalability.
▌      * **Takeaways**:
▌          * Our observability `METRIC`s should include context IDs (e.g., `graph_id`, `op_id`) that allow user-space tools to
▌reconstruct the full causal chain of an event.
▌          * The kernel should provide the tracing *mechanism* (high-resolution timestamps, tracepoints), while user-space
▌handles collection and analysis.
▌
▌4.  **Borg, Omega, and Kubernetes: Lessons learned from three container management systems** (2016, ACM Queue)
▌
▌      * **Annotation**: Describes the evolution of cluster schedulers at Google, highlighting the move towards optimistic
▌scheduling and separating policy from mechanism.
▌      * **Takeaways**:
▌          * For the P3 SSI, the kernel should provide placement *primitives*, but allow a user-space scheduler to make the
▌actual placement *decisions* based on richer application-level context.
▌          * Avoid overly centralized control; our minimal Raft consensus should only manage critical shared state like
▌cluster membership, not per-operator scheduling.
▌
▌-----
▌
▌## Decision Pack: Key Architectural Choices
▌
▌1.  **Decision: Adopt a pure Dataflow/Graph-based scheduling model, abandoning traditional threads.**
▌
▌      * **Pros**: Eliminates entire classes of concurrency bugs (race conditions, deadlocks); provides natural backpressure;
▌execution is highly analyzable and lends itself to determinism.
▌      * **Cons**: Unfamiliar programming model; not suitable for all general-purpose workloads (but this is an AI-native
▌kernel).
▌      * **Recommendation**: **Adopt.** This is the core architectural identity of the project and the foundation of its value
▌proposition.
▌
▌2.  **Decision: Use Capabilities as the *only* access control mechanism.**
▌
▌      * **Pros**: Unified, simple, and powerful security model; enforces principle of least privilege by default; aligns with
▌microkernel best practices (seL4).
▌      * **Cons**: Can be complex to manage capability derivation and revocation in user-space.
▌      * **Recommendation**: **Adopt.** A unified security model is essential for a minimal kernel. The complexity can be
▌managed by well-designed user-space libraries.
▌
▌3.  **Decision: Strictly separate consensus from the data plane in the multi-node design.**
▌
▌      * **Pros**: Keeps the high-throughput data path free from high-latency consensus protocols; improves performance and
▌scalability; simplifies the dataflow logic.
▌      * **Cons**: The control plane becomes a single point of failure for placement decisions (though Raft provides fault
▌tolerance for the control plane itself).
▌      * **Recommendation**: **Adopt.** The performance benefits of a consensus-free data plane are too significant to ignore
▌for an AI-native kernel.
▌
▌Grok :
▌### Phase 1: Core Data Structures, Algorithms, Pseudocode/Code, METRICs
▌
▌Focus on dataflow-first design with zero-copy tensors, bounded channels for backpressure, and operator scheduling. These
▌build on Rust's ownership for safety in no_std, integrating with SIS's AI-native vDSO for tensor paths. Algorithms prioritize
▌lock-free where possible for HYPERCUBE scaling, with AArch64 atomics for ordering.
▌
▌#### Zero-Copy Tensor Memory
▌Use slab pools for allocation, with lifetimes tied to scopes via Rust's borrow checker. Versioning via immutable snapshots
▌(clone-on-write semantics). Safe wrappers: Use `&'a mut [u8]` for raw data, aligned to cache lines (64 bytes on AArch64). For
▌NUMA (future), add affinity hints. Algorithm: Pre-allocate static slabs, track free slots with bitmap (lock-free via
▌atomics).
▌
▌Pseudocode:
▌```
▌Initialize slab: array of fixed-size blocks, bitmap for free/used.
▌Allocate: Find free bit (atomic CAS), return slice.
▌Deallocate: Atomic clear bit.
▌Version: On modify, CAS version counter; if conflict, copy to new slab.
▌```
▌
▌Rust Snippet (no_std, AArch64-aware):
▌```rust
▌use core::sync::atomic::{AtomicU64, Ordering};
▌use core::mem::align_of;
▌
▌const CACHE_LINE: usize = 64;
▌const SLAB_SIZE: usize = 1024; // Tune for kernel
▌
▌#[repr(align(64))] // Cache-line align
▌struct TensorSlab {
▌    data: [u8; SLAB_SIZE],
▌    version: AtomicU64,
▌    free_bitmap: AtomicU64, // Bitmask for slots
▌}
▌
▌impl TensorSlab {
▌    fn alloc(&self, size: usize) -> Option<&'static mut [u8]> {
▌        let slot = size.next_power_of_two().trailing_zeros() as u64; // Simple size class
▌        let old = self.free_bitmap.load(Ordering::Acquire);
▌        let mask = 1u64 << slot;
▌        if old & mask == 0 {
▌            if self.free_bitmap.compare_exchange(old, old | mask, Ordering::AcqRel, Ordering::Acquire).is_ok() {
▌                // DSB for AArch64 ordering
▌                unsafe { asm!("dsb sy"); }
▌                Some(&mut self.data[slot as usize * size..(slot as usize + 1) * size])
▌            } else {
▌                None
▌            }
▌        } else {
▌            None
▌        }
▌    }
▌
▌    fn deallocate(&self, ptr: *mut u8) {
▌        let offset = (ptr as usize - self.data.as_ptr() as usize) / SLAB_SIZE;
▌        let mask = !(1u64 << offset);
▌        self.free_bitmap.fetch_and(mask, Ordering::Release);
▌        // ISB for flush
▌        unsafe { asm!("isb"); }
▌    }
▌}
▌```
▌METRICs: Allocation latency (<100ns P99 via PMU L1 miss count), hit rate (>95%), version conflicts (<1% under load).
▌
▌#### Bounded Channels with Backpressure
▌SPSC for single-producer (fastest, lock-free), MPMC for multi (with credits). Priority: Heapless queues with levels (e.g.,
▌0-3). Choose SPSC for intra-core tensor flows (zero fences), MPMC for inter-operator with credits to avoid overflow. AArch64
▌ordering: Acquire/Release for visibility, DSB for strong barriers in critical paths.
▌
▌Pseudocode:
▌```
▌SPSC: Ring buffer with head/tail atomics.
▌Enqueue: If full (head == tail + capacity), backpressure (yield).
▌Dequeue: Load-acquire tail, advance with release.
▌MPMC: Add credit counter; producer acquires credit before enqueue.
▌```
▌
▌Rust Snippet (lock-free SPSC):
▌```rust
▌use core::sync::atomic::{AtomicUsize, Ordering};
▌use core::ptr::NonNull;
▌
▌struct SpscQueue<T, const N: usize> {
▌    buffer: [T; N],
▌    head: AtomicUsize,
▌    tail: AtomicUsize,
▌}
▌
▌impl<T: Copy, const N: usize> SpscQueue<T, N> {
▌    fn enqueue(&self, value: T) -> Result<(), T> {
▌        let tail = self.tail.load(Ordering::Relaxed);
▌        let head = self.head.load(Ordering::Acquire);
▌        if (tail + 1) % N == head { return Err(value); } // Full, backpressure
▌        self.buffer[tail] = value;
▌        self.tail.store((tail + 1) % N, Ordering::Release);
▌        Ok(())
▌    }
▌
▌    fn dequeue(&self) -> Option<T> {
▌        let head = self.head.load(Ordering::Relaxed);
▌        let tail = self.tail.load(Ordering::Acquire);
▌        if head == tail { return None; }
▌        let value = self.buffer[head];
▌        self.head.store((head + 1) % N, Ordering::Release);
▌        Some(value)
▌    }
▌}
▌```
▌METRICs: Throughput (>1M ops/sec per core), latency (<200ns enqueue P99), backpressure events (<5% under peak).
▌
▌#### Operator Scheduling Loop
▌Run-to-completion for simple graphs (low overhead), cooperative yields for long-running ops. Heuristics: Co-schedule
▌dependent operators on same core to minimize cache misses. Starvation avoidance: Round-robin fallback after N yields.
▌
▌Pseudocode:
▌```
▌Loop: Select ready operator (priority queue).
▌Execute until yield or complete.
▌On yield: Check deadlines, reschedule.
▌Co-schedule: If dep chain, pin to core.
▌```
▌
▌Rust Snippet:
▌```rust
▌struct Operator {
▌    id: usize,
▌    deps: [usize; MAX_DEPS],
▌    priority: u32,
▌}
▌
▌fn schedule(ops: &[Operator]) {
▌    let mut ready = AtomicUsize::new(0); // Bitmask
▌    loop {
▌        let id = find_highest_prio_ready(&ready);
▌        if id.is_none() { break; } // No ready
▌        execute_op(id.unwrap(), &ops[id.unwrap()]);
▌        // Yield point: Check if long-running
▌        if should_yield() { // Cycle count > threshold
▌            yield_cpu(); // ARM64 WFI
▌        }
▌    }
▌}
▌```
▌METRICs: Completion time variance (<5% jitter), co-schedule hit rate (>80%), starvation incidents (0 under test loads).
▌
▌### Phase 2: Deterministic Scheduler & Capabilities, Pseudocode/Code, METRICs
▌
▌#### Deterministic Scheduling (EDF/Hybrid)
▌EDF for deadlines: Priority = 1/deadline. Hybrid: EDF for real-time, round-robin for best-effort. Data structures: Binary
▌heap for tasks, sorted by absolute deadline. Timer: Use ARM64 CNTVCT_EL0 for precise interrupts. Preemption: Mask IRQs during
▌critical sections (<10μs windows). Admission: Sum util <=1 (WCET/deadline). Pinned cores for predictability.
▌
▌Pseudocode:
▌```
▌Enqueue: Insert into heap by deadline.
▌Dequeue: Pop earliest.
▌Admission: If sum(WCET_i / period_i) > 1, reject.
▌Preempt: On timer IRQ, check if current > next deadline, switch.
▌```
▌
▌Rust Snippet (EDF Heap):
▌```rust
▌use core::cmp::Ordering as Ord;
▌
▌struct Task {
▌    deadline: u64, // Absolute
▌    wcet: u64,
▌}
▌
▌struct EdfHeap {
▌    tasks: [Task; MAX_TASKS],
▌    size: usize,
▌}
▌
▌impl EdfHeap {
▌    fn insert(&mut self, task: Task) {
▌        self.tasks[self.size] = task;
▌        self.heapify_up(self.size);
▌        self.size += 1;
▌    }
▌
▌    fn pop(&mut self) -> Option<Task> {
▌        if self.size == 0 { return None; }
▌        let root = self.tasks[0];
▌        self.size -= 1;
▌        self.tasks[0] = self.tasks[self.size];
▌        self.heapify_down(0);
▌        Some(root)
▌    }
▌
▌    fn heapify_up(&mut self, mut i: usize) {
▌        while i > 0 {
▌            let p = (i - 1) / 2;
▌            if self.tasks[i].deadline < self.tasks[p].deadline { // Min-heap
▌                self.tasks.swap(i, p);
▌                i = p;
▌            } else {
▌                break;
▌            }
▌        }
▌    }
▌
▌    fn heapify_down(&mut self, mut i: usize) {
▌        loop {
▌            let l = 2 * i + 1;
▌            let r = 2 * i + 2;
▌            let mut smallest = i;
▌            if l < self.size && self.tasks[l].deadline < self.tasks[smallest].deadline {
▌                smallest = l;
▌            }
▌            if r < self.size && self.tasks[r].deadline < self.tasks[smallest].deadline {
▌                smallest = r;
▌            }
▌            if smallest != i {
▌                self.tasks.swap(i, smallest);
▌                i = smallest;
▌            } else {
▌                break;
▌            }
▌        }
▌    }
▌}
▌```
▌Admission Control:
▌```rust
▌fn admit(task: &Task) -> bool {
▌    let util = task.wcet as f64 / task.period as f64; // Assume period = deadline for EDF
▌    if current_util + util > 1.0 {
▌        false
▌    } else {
▌        current_util += util;
▌        true
▌    }
▌}
▌```
▌METRICs: Schedulability (>95% admitted under load), jitter (<1% deadline miss rate), preempt overhead (<200ns).
▌
▌#### Capability System
▌Table: Hashmap-like with tags (sealed bits). Fast checks: Inline tag validation. Metadata: Version, permissions.
▌Verification: ECDSA signatures on load. TEE hook: Future enclave calls.
▌
▌Pseudocode:
▌```
▌Cap: ID, tag (sealed), perms.
▌Check: If tag invalid, revoke.
▌Verify: Hash + sig check on package.
▌```
▌
▌Rust Snippet:
▌```rust
▌struct Cap {
▌    id: u64,
▌    tag: u64, // Sealed with kernel key
▌    perms: u32,
▌}
▌
▌fn check_cap(cap: &Cap) -> bool {
▌    (cap.tag & SEAL_MASK) == expected_seal // Constant-time
▌}
▌
▌fn verify_package(pkg: &[u8]) -> bool {
▌    let hash = sha256(pkg);
▌    ecdsa_verify(&hash, &sig) // Using ecdsa crate
▌}
▌```
▌METRICs: Check latency (<50ns), verification time (<1ms per package), revoke rate (0 under normal).
▌
▌### Phase 3: Minimal RPC & Placement, Pseudocode/Code, METRICs
▌
▌#### Minimal RPC Fabric
▌Over virtio-net: Framed messages (header: seqID, len, CRC). Congestion: Token bucket backpressure. Retry: Exponential backoff
▌(<100ms timeout). Zero-copy: Map NIC buffers directly to tensors.
▌
▌Pseudocode:
▌```
▌Send: Header + data, CRC append.
▌Recv: Read header, verify CRC, ack.
▌Backpressure: If tokens=0, wait.
▌Retry: On nack, backoff *2.
▌```
▌
▌Rust Snippet (Send/Recv):
▌```rust
▌struct RpcHeader {
▌    seq: u64,
▌    len: u32,
▌    crc: u32,
▌}
▌
▌fn send_rpc(net: &VirtioNet, data: &[u8]) -> Result<(), Error> {
▌    let mut buf = [0u8; HEADER_SIZE + data.len()];
▌    let header = RpcHeader { seq: next_seq(), len: data.len() as u32, crc: 0 };
▌    buf[0..HEADER_SIZE].copy_from_slice(&header.as_bytes());
▌    buf[HEADER_SIZE..].copy_from_slice(data);
▌    header.crc = crc32(&buf); // Update CRC
▌    net.send(&buf); // Zero-copy if mapped
▌    Ok(())
▌}
▌
▌fn recv_rpc(net: &VirtioNet) -> Vec<u8> {
▌    let buf = net.recv();
▌    let header = RpcHeader::from_bytes(&buf[0..HEADER_SIZE]);
▌    if crc32(&buf) != header.crc { retry(); }
▌    buf[HEADER_SIZE..HEADER_SIZE + header.len as usize].to_vec()
▌}
▌```
▌METRICs: Throughput (>10Gbps), latency (<100μs E2E), retry rate (<1%).
▌
▌#### Graph Placement Fast Path
▌First: Pipeline parallelism (place sequential ops on same node). Heuristics: Batch per-operator if >threshold. Failure:
▌Idempotent replay via seqIDs.
▌
▌Pseudocode:
▌```
▌Placement: For graph, score nodes by bandwidth/latency.
▌Assign: Greedy, place deps close.
▌Replay: On fail, resend from checkpoint.
▌```
▌
▌Rust Snippet:
▌```rust
▌fn place_graph(graph: &Graph) -> NodeAssignment {
▌    let mut assign = vec![0; graph.nodes.len()];
▌    for i in 0..graph.nodes.len() {
▌        let best_node = find_min_latency(graph.deps[i]);
▌        assign[i] = best_node;
▌    }
▌    assign
▌}
▌```
▌METRICs: Placement time (<1ms), parallelism gain (2x speedup), recovery <50ms.
▌
▌### Bench/Validation Plan
▌Microbenches: Use criterion.rs (no_std port) for channels/schedulers (10k iterations, warm-up 100). METRICs: P50/P95/P99
▌latencies, variance <5%. For QEMU: Use -icount for deterministic cycles. CI: Thresholds (e.g., inference <40μs or fail).
▌Validation: Compare to Linux (LMbench) for baselines.
▌
▌### Pitfalls & Mitigations
▌- **AArch64 Memory Model**: Weak ordering; pitfall: Missing DSB/ISB leads to stale data. Mitigate: Use Acquire/Release, fence
▌on critical (e.g., after store in queues).
▌- **QEMU Artifacts**: Non-deterministic timing; mitigate: -icount shift=0 for cycle-accurate, average 100 runs.
▌- **Lock Contention vs. Cache Thrash**: False sharing; mitigate: Pad atomics to cache lines (#[repr(align(64)]).
▌- **TLB/Cache**: Jitter from misses; mitigate: Pre-warm with dummy accesses, PMU-guided (L1D miss count <1%).
▌
▌### References with Actionable Takeaways
▌- **Lock-Free Queues**: "A Lock-Free Ring Buffer in Rust: Design and Implementation" (Medium, 2025). Takeaways: Use AtomicPtr
▌for nodes to avoid ABA (apply to SPSC with CAS); benchmark contention with 147% SIMD speedup; pad to 64B for false sharing.
▌- **High-Throughput RPC**: "Io_uring, kTLS and Rust for zero syscall HTTPS server" (HN, 2025). Takeaways: Zero-syscall with
▌io_uring equiv in virtio (implement polling loops); >100Gbit throughput via batching; use credit for backpressure.
▌- **AArch64 Memory Ordering**: "ARM64 Memory Ordering" (ElseWhere, 2023). Takeaways: Use DMB/DSB for strong barriers in
▌queues (add after stores); avoid over-fencing (profile with PMU); pitfalls like reordering in weak model.
▌- **PMU Usage**: "Using ARM Performance Monitor Unit (PMU) Linux Driver" (Arm Community, 2015). Takeaways: EL1 programming
▌for counters (implement in EL1 mode); map to events like L1 misses; avoid bias by sampling <1% overhead.
▌- **EDF Implementations**: "Scheduling Algorithms for Real-Time and Embedded Systems KERNEL" (Academia.edu, 2025). Takeaways:
▌Hybrid EDF/RM for mixed loads (implement admission sum<1); use binary heaps for O(log n) insert; proofs for schedulability.
▌- **Deterministic Real-Time Techniques**: "How to Achieve Deterministic Behavior in Real-Time Embedded
▌Systems" (EmbeddedRelated, 2025). Takeaways: Pre-warm caches for jitter control (add dummy loops); pinned cores for
▌determinism; p99 bounds via statistical runs.

▌# AI-Native Kernel: Architecture Blueprint & Implementation Roadmap
▌
▌## Executive Plan
▌
▌### Vision Statement
▌Transform the SIS kernel from a metrics-capable boot environment into a research-grade AI-native OS where dataflow graphs,
▌tensors, and models are first-class kernel objects with deterministic execution guarantees and distributed capabilities.
▌
▌### Key Recommendations
▌1. **Dataflow-First Architecture**: Implement kernel objects (Operator, Tensor, Channel) with zero-copy semantics and static
▌graph compilation
▌2. **Deterministic Scheduling**: CBS-EDF hybrid scheduler with admission control and deadline enforcement
▌3. **Model Capabilities**: Capability-based security with signed model packages and measurement chains
▌4. **Structured Observability**: PMU-aligned tracepoints with operator-level attribution
▌5. **Minimal SSI**: RPC-based multi-node with placement hints and eventual consistency
▌
▌### 12-Week Core Roadmap + 8-Week Advanced
▌
▌**Weeks 1-3: Dataflow Foundation**
▌- Implement core kernel objects (Operator, Tensor, Channel)
▌- Zero-copy tensor passing with reference counting

▌
▌**Weeks 4-6: Deterministic Scheduling**

▌- Timer discipline and jitter control
▌- **Milestone**: <10μs scheduling jitter, proven via 1000-run CI
▌
▌**Weeks 7-9: Model Security**

▌**Weeks 13-16: Multi-Node SSI**

▌## 1. Dataflow Kernel Architecture
▌
▌### Minimal Kernel Objects
▌
▌```rust

▌pub struct KernelGraph {
▌    operators: BTreeMap<OperatorId, Operator>,

▌    schedule: CompiledSchedule,
▌}
▌

▌

▌    shape: TensorShape,

▌
▌### Zero-Copy Tensor Implementation
▌
▌```rust
▌// Zero-copy tensor passing with COW semantics
▌impl Tensor {
▌    pub fn share(&self) -> Result<TensorRef, Error> {
▌        if self.refcount.fetch_add(1, Ordering::AcqRel) > MAX_REFS {
▌            return Err(Error::TooManyRefs);
▌        }
▌
▌        Ok(TensorRef {
▌            tensor_id: self.id,
▌            version: self.version,
▌            read_only: true,
▌        })
▌    }
▌
▌    pub fn make_writable(&mut self) -> Result<(), Error> {
▌        if self.refcount.load(Ordering::Acquire) > 1 {
▌            // COW: Allocate new pages and copy
▌            let new_pages = self.cow_duplicate()?;
▌            self.data = new_pages;
▌            self.version += 1;
▌        }
▌        Ok(())
▌    }
▌}
▌
▌// Memory layout for zero-copy
▌#[repr(C, align(64))]  // Cache-line aligned
▌pub struct TensorHeader {
▌    magic: u32,
▌    version: u32,
▌    shape: [u64; 4],
▌    stride: [u64; 4],
▌    dtype: u32,
▌    flags: u32,
▌    data_offset: u64,
▌}
▌```
▌
▌### Backpressure Design
▌
▌```rust
▌pub enum BackpressurePolicy {
▌    DropOldest,
▌    DropNewest,
▌    Block { timeout_us: u64 },
▌    Adaptive { target_depth: usize },
▌}
▌
▌impl Channel {
▌    pub fn send(&mut self, tensor: TensorRef) -> Result<(), SendError> {
▌        if self.queue.is_full() {
▌            match self.backpressure {
▌                BackpressurePolicy::DropOldest => {
▌                    self.queue.pop_front();
▌                    self.metrics.dropped_tensors += 1;
▌                }
▌                BackpressurePolicy::Block { timeout_us } => {
▌                    self.waiters.wait_with_timeout(timeout_us)?;
▌                }
▌                BackpressurePolicy::Adaptive { target_depth } => {
▌                    self.apply_adaptive_pressure(target_depth);
▌                }
▌                _ => {}
▌            }
▌        }
▌
▌        self.queue.push_back(tensor)?;
▌        self.waiters.wake_one();
▌        Ok(())
▌    }
▌}
▌```
▌
▌### Scheduling Policy Evolution
▌
▌**Stage 1: Static Priority (Weeks 1-3)**
▌```rust
▌pub struct StaticScheduler {
▌    priority_queues: [RunQueue; 32],
▌    graph_order: Vec<OperatorId>,  // Topological sort
▌}
▌```
▌
▌**Stage 2: CBS-EDF Hybrid (Weeks 4-6)**
▌```rust
▌pub struct CBSEDFScheduler {
▌    deadline_queue: BinaryHeap<DeadlineTask>,
▌    bandwidth_servers: Vec<CBSServer>,
▌    admission_control: AdmissionController,
▌}
▌
▌impl CBSEDFScheduler {
▌    pub fn admit_task(&mut self, task: Task) -> Result<(), AdmissionError> {
▌        let utilization = task.wcet as f64 / task.period as f64;
▌        if self.total_utilization() + utilization > 0.85 {  // 85% bound
▌            return Err(AdmissionError::InsufficientBandwidth);
▌        }
▌
▌        self.deadline_queue.push(DeadlineTask {
▌            absolute_deadline: now() + task.period,
▌            task,
▌        });
▌        Ok(())
▌    }
▌}
▌```
▌
▌**References:**
▌- [Abeni & Buttazzo, "Integrating Multimedia Applications in Hard Real-Time Systems" (RTSS 1998)](https://
▌ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/739726) - CBS server design for mixed workloads. **Takeaway**: Use bandwidth servers to isolate
▌AI inference from system tasks.
▌- [TensorFlow TFRT](https://github.com/tensorflow/runtime) - Graph executor design. **Takeaway**: Static graph compilation
▌reduces runtime overhead; adopt their BEF format concepts.

▌## 2. Determinism and Timing

▌### Deterministic Mode Structure
▌
▌```rust
▌pub struct DeterministicMode {
▌    fixed_tick_source: FixedTimer,
▌    pinned_cores: CpuSet,
▌    banned_operations: BTreeSet<Syscall>,
▌    cache_partitions: Vec<CachePartition>,
▌}
▌
▌impl DeterministicMode {
▌    pub fn enter(&mut self) -> Result<(), Error> {
▌        // 1. Disable dynamic frequency scaling
▌        cpu::set_frequency_fixed(2_400_000);  // 2.4GHz
▌
▌        // 2. Pin interrupts away from RT cores
▌        gic::set_affinity_mask(self.pinned_cores.invert());
▌
▌        // 3. Partition caches
▌        for partition in &self.cache_partitions {
▌            arm64::set_cache_partition(partition)?;
▌        }
▌
▌        // 4. Disable preemption on RT cores
▌        for cpu in self.pinned_cores.iter() {
▌            per_cpu(cpu).preempt_disable();
▌        }
▌
▌        Ok(())
▌    }
▌}
▌```

▌### Jitter Control for Inference
▌
▌```rust
▌pub struct InferenceLoop {
▌    warmup_iterations: u32,
▌    timer: HighResTimer,
▌    pmu_config: PMUConfig,
▌}
▌
▌impl InferenceLoop {
▌    pub fn execute_deterministic(&mut self, graph: &Graph) -> MetricsReport {
▌        // Cache warming
▌        for _ in 0..self.warmup_iterations {
▌            graph.dry_run();
▌        }
▌
▌        // Disable interrupts for critical section
▌        let _irq_guard = irq::disable();
▌
▌        // Start PMU counters
▌        self.pmu_config.reset_and_start();
▌
▌        // Execute with precise timing
▌        let start = self.timer.read_cycles();
▌        graph.execute();
▌        let end = self.timer.read_cycles();
▌
▌        // Collect PMU data
▌        let pmu_data = self.pmu_config.read_all();
▌
▌        MetricsReport {
▌            cycles: end - start,
▌            instructions: pmu_data.instructions,
▌            cache_misses: pmu_data.l1d_misses,
▌            branch_misses: pmu_data.branch_misses,
▌        }
▌    }
▌}
▌```

▌### Reproducibility Methodology
▌
▌```rust
▌pub struct ReproducibilityTest {
▌    seed: u64,
▌    iterations: u32,
▌    tolerance_ns: u64,
▌}
▌
▌impl ReproducibilityTest {
▌    pub fn validate(&self) -> ValidationResult {
▌        let mut timings = Vec::with_capacity(self.iterations as usize);
▌
▌        for i in 0..self.iterations {
▌            // Reset to known state
▌            kernel::reset_to_checkpoint();
▌            rng::seed(self.seed + i as u64);
▌
▌            // Run identical workload
▌            let timing = self.run_workload();
▌            timings.push(timing);
▌        }
▌
▌        // Calculate statistics
▌        let mean = statistical::mean(&timings);
▌        let stddev = statistical::stddev(&timings);
▌        let max_jitter = timings.iter().max().unwrap() - timings.iter().min().unwrap();
▌
▌        ValidationResult {
▌            deterministic: max_jitter < self.tolerance_ns,
▌            mean_ns: mean,
▌            stddev_ns: stddev,
▌            max_jitter_ns: max_jitter,
▌        }
▌    }
▌}
▌```
▌
▌**References:**
▌- [Lelli et al., "An efficient and scalable implementation of global EDF in Linux" (RTLWS 2011)](https://lwn.net/
▌Articles/471613/) - Linux SCHED_DEADLINE implementation. **Takeaway**: Admission control prevents overload; use their
▌utilization bound calculations.
▌- [ARM Cache Partitioning Guide](https://developer.arm.com/documentation/102336/0100) - Hardware cache isolation.
▌**Takeaway**: Use MPAM for cache/bandwidth partitioning when available.

▌        const INSPECT_WEIGHTS = 0x008;

▌        const ATTEST = 0x040;

▌impl ModelCapability {
▌    pub fn check_operation(&self, op: ModelOperation) -> Result<(), PermissionError> {

▌            ModelOperation::LoadWeights(size) => {
▌                if !self.permissions.contains(ModelPermissions::LOAD) {
▌                    return Err(PermissionError::NoLoadPermission);
▌                }
▌                if size > self.constraints.max_memory_mb * 1024 * 1024 {
▌                    return Err(PermissionError::MemoryLimitExceeded);
▌                }
▌            }
▌            ModelOperation::Execute(input) => {
▌                self.check_data_access(&input)?;
▌                self.check_compute_budget()?;
▌            }
▌            _ => {}
▌        }
▌        Ok(())
▌    }
▌}

▌### Signed Model Packages
▌
▌```rust
▌pub struct SignedModelPackage {
▌    header: PackageHeader,
▌    manifest: Manifest,
▌    model_data: Vec<u8>,
▌    signature: Ed25519Signature,
▌}
▌
▌#[repr(C)]
▌pub struct PackageHeader {
▌    magic: [u8; 4],  // "SMDL"
▌    version: u32,
▌    hash_algorithm: u32,
▌    model_hash: [u8; 32],
▌    manifest_offset: u64,
▌    data_offset: u64,
▌}
▌
▌pub struct Manifest {
▌    model_id: Uuid,
▌    author: String,
▌    timestamp: u64,
▌    dependencies: Vec<Dependency>,
▌    permissions_requested: ModelPermissions,
▌    attestation_policy: AttestationPolicy,
▌}
▌
▌impl SignedModelPackage {
▌    pub fn verify_and_load(&self, pubkey: &PublicKey) -> Result<Model, Error> {
▌        // 1. Verify signature
▌        let message = self.get_signed_content();
▌        if !ed25519::verify(&self.signature, &message, pubkey) {
▌            return Err(Error::InvalidSignature);
▌        }
▌
▌        // 2. Verify hash chain
▌        let computed_hash = sha256(&self.model_data);
▌        if computed_hash != self.header.model_hash {
▌            return Err(Error::HashMismatch);
▌        }
▌
▌        // 3. Record measurement for attestation
▌        MEASUREMENT_LOG.record(ModelMeasurement {
▌            model_id: self.manifest.model_id,
▌            hash: computed_hash,
▌            timestamp: now(),
▌        });
▌
▌        // 4. Load with constraints
▌        Model::load_with_constraints(
▌            &self.model_data,
▌            &self.manifest.permissions_requested,
▌        )
▌    }
▌}
▌```
▌
▌### Secure Model Store
▌
▌```rust
▌pub struct SecureModelStore {
▌    encryption_key: AesKey,
▌    storage_backend: StorageBackend,
▌    version_tree: MerkleTree,
▌}
▌
▌impl SecureModelStore {
▌    pub fn store_model(&mut self, model: &Model) -> Result<ModelHandle, Error> {
▌        // 1. Encrypt model data
▌        let encrypted = aes_gcm::encrypt(&model.serialize(), &self.encryption_key)?;
▌
▌        // 2. Version control with Merkle tree
▌        let version = self.version_tree.next_version();
▌        let node = MerkleNode {
▌            version,
▌            hash: sha256(&encrypted),
▌            parent: self.version_tree.current_root(),
▌        };
▌        self.version_tree.insert(node);
▌
▌        // 3. Store with rollback protection
▌        let handle = ModelHandle {
▌            id: model.id,
▌            version,
▌            merkle_proof: self.version_tree.get_proof(version),
▌        };
▌
▌        self.storage_backend.store(handle.storage_key(), encrypted)?;
▌
▌        Ok(handle)
▌    }
▌}
▌```
▌
▌**References:**
▌- [Watson et al., "CHERI: A Hybrid Capability-System Architecture" (IEEE S&P 2015)](https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/research/
▌security/ctsrd/pdfs/201505-ieee-cheri.pdf) - Capability-based security. **Takeaway**: Fine-grained capabilities prevent
▌confused deputy attacks.
▌- [Microsoft SEAL](https://github.com/microsoft/SEAL) - Homomorphic encryption for ML. **Takeaway**: Consider FHE for
▌privacy-preserving inference in future iterations.

▌### PMU Integration
▌
▌```rust
▌pub struct OperatorPMUAttribution {
▌    counters: PerCpuCounters,
▌    operator_map: BTreeMap<OperatorId, PMUSnapshot>,
▌}
▌
▌impl OperatorPMUAttribution {
▌    pub fn measure_operator<F>(&mut self, op_id: OperatorId, f: F) -> OperatorMetrics
▌    where
▌        F: FnOnce(),
▌    {
▌        // Save current context
▌        let prev = self.counters.read_all();
▌
▌        // Configure PMU for operator profiling
▌        arm64::pmu::configure(&[
▌            PMUEvent::CPU_CYCLES,
▌            PMUEvent::INSTRUCTIONS,
▌            PMUEvent::L1D_CACHE_MISS,
▌            PMUEvent::BRANCH_MISS,
▌        ]);
▌
▌        // Execute operator
▌        arm64::pmu::reset();
▌        arm64::pmu::start();
▌        f();
▌        arm64::pmu::stop();
▌
▌        // Read counters
▌        let snapshot = PMUSnapshot {
▌            cycles: arm64::pmu::read(0),
▌            instructions: arm64::pmu::read(1),
▌            l1d_misses: arm64::pmu::read(2),
▌            branch_misses: arm64::pmu::read(3),
▌        };
▌
▌        // Restore context
▌        self.counters.restore(prev);
▌
▌        // Record attribution
▌        self.operator_map.insert(op_id, snapshot);
▌
▌        OperatorMetrics::from_pmu(snapshot)
▌    }
▌}
▌```

▌### Placement Heuristics
▌
▌```rust
▌pub struct PlacementEngine {
▌    cost_model: CostModel,
▌    node_capabilities: BTreeMap<NodeId, NodeCapabilities>,
▌}
▌
▌impl PlacementEngine {
▌    pub fn partition_graph(&self, graph: &Graph) -> GraphPartitioning {
▌        // 1. Identify pipeline stages
▌        let stages = self.identify_pipeline_stages(graph);
▌
▌        // 2. Calculate data transfer costs
▌        let transfer_matrix = self.calculate_transfer_costs(&stages);
▌
▌        // 3. Apply min-cut partitioning
▌        let partitions = self.min_cut_partition(&stages, &transfer_matrix);
▌
▌        // 4. Assign to nodes based on capabilities
▌        let mut assignment = GraphPartitioning::new();
▌
▌        for partition in partitions {
▌            let best_node = self.find_best_node(&partition);
▌            assignment.assign(partition, best_node);
▌        }
▌
▌        // 5. Insert communication operators
▌        self.insert_remote_channels(&mut assignment);
▌
▌        assignment
▌    }
▌
▌    fn calculate_affinity_score(&self, op: &Operator, node: NodeId) -> f64 {
▌        let node_cap = &self.node_capabilities[&node];
▌
▌        let compute_match = match op.kind {
▌            OperatorKind::MatMul => node_cap.tensor_cores as f64,
▌            OperatorKind::Conv2D => node_cap.conv_accelerator as f64,
▌            _ => 1.0,
▌        };
▌
▌        let memory_fit = if op.memory_required() < node_cap.available_memory {
▌            1.0
▌        } else {
▌            0.1
▌        };
▌
▌        compute_match * memory_fit * node_cap.load_factor()
▌    }
▌}
▌```

▌### Fault Detection
▌
▌```rust
▌pub struct FaultDetector {
▌    heartbeat_interval: Duration,
▌    timeout: Duration,
▌    node_states: BTreeMap<NodeId, NodeState>,
▌}
▌
▌impl FaultDetector {
▌    pub async fn monitor_nodes(&mut self) {
▌        loop {
▌            tokio::time::sleep(self.heartbeat_interval).await;
▌
▌            for (node_id, state) in &mut self.node_states {
▌                if state.last_heartbeat.elapsed() > self.timeout {
▌                    self.handle_node_failure(*node_id).await;
▌                }
▌            }
▌        }
▌    }
▌
▌    async fn handle_node_failure(&mut self, failed_node: NodeId) {
▌        // 1. Mark node as failed
▌        self.node_states.get_mut(&failed_node).unwrap().status = NodeStatus::Failed;
▌
▌        // 2. Identify affected graphs
▌        let affected = self.find_affected_graphs(failed_node);
▌
▌        // 3. Trigger re-placement
▌        for graph_id in affected {
▌            self.trigger_graph_migration(graph_id, failed_node).await;
▌        }
▌
▌        // 4. Emit metrics
▌        METRICS.node_failures.inc();
▌    }
▌}
▌```

▌```rust
▌pub struct ValidationThresholds {

▌    hardware: ThresholdSet,

▌### Reproducibility Framework
▌
▌```rust
▌pub struct ReproducibleRun {
▌    config: RunConfig,
▌    seed: u64,
▌    inputs: Vec<TestInput>,
▌}
▌
▌impl ReproducibleRun {
▌    pub fn execute(&self) -> RunResult {
▌        // 1. Snapshot configuration
▌        let config_hash = sha256(&bincode::serialize(&self.config).unwrap());
▌
▌        // 2. Initialize deterministic environment
▌        kernel::set_deterministic_mode(true);
▌        rng::seed(self.seed);
▌
▌        // 3. Run with fixed inputs
▌        let mut results = Vec::new();
▌        for input in &self.inputs {
▌            let output = self.run_workload(input);
▌            results.push(output);
▌        }
▌
▌        // 4. Generate reproducibility package
▌        RunResult {
▌            config_hash,
▌            seed: self.seed,
▌            results,
▌            metrics: self.collect_metrics(),
▌            reproducibility_score: self.calculate_reproducibility(&results),
▌        }
▌    }
▌}

▌**References:**
▌- [Mytkowicz et al., "Producing Wrong Data Without Doing Anything Obviously Wrong!" (ASPLOS 2009)](https://dl.acm.org/
▌doi/10.1145/1508244.1508275) - Measurement bias. **Takeaway**: Control for environment variables; use multiple runs with
▌different link orders.
▌
▌## Decision Pack
▌
▌### Decision 1: Graph Execution Model
▌**Options:**
▌- A) Dynamic dataflow with runtime scheduling
▌- B) Static compilation with fixed schedule
▌- C) Hybrid with JIT optimization
▌
▌**Recommendation: B (Static compilation)**
▌- **Pros**: Predictable latency, minimal runtime overhead, easier verification
▌- **Cons**: Less flexible, requires recompilation for changes
▌- **Rationale**: Aligns with determinism goals and embedded AI use cases
▌
▌### Decision 2: Memory Management
▌**Options:**
▌- A) Traditional malloc/free with heap
▌- B) Region-based with arenas
▌- C) Pure stack allocation with static limits
▌
▌**Recommendation: B (Region-based)**
▌- **Pros**: Predictable allocation time, no fragmentation, bulk deallocation
▌- **Cons**: Potential memory waste, requires careful region planning
▌- **Rationale**: Best balance of performance and predictability for AI workloads
▌
▌### Decision 3: Multi-Node Consistency
▌**Options:**
▌- A) Strong consistency with Raft
▌- B) Eventual consistency with CRDTs
▌- C) Weak consistency with best-effort
▌
▌**Recommendation: B (Eventual consistency)**
▌- **Pros**: Better performance, partition tolerance, sufficient for AI workloads
▌- **Cons**: Complex reasoning about state, potential temporary inconsistency
▌- **Rationale**: AI models tolerate some inconsistency; performance is critical
▌
▌### Decision 4: Security Model
▌**Options:**
▌- A) Full capability system from day 1
▌- B) Simple ACLs initially, capabilities later
▌- C) No security initially, add later
▌
▌**Recommendation: A (Full capability system)**
▌- **Pros**: Security by design, no retrofit needed, clean architecture
▌- **Cons**: Higher initial complexity, longer development time
▌- **Rationale**: Security is fundamental to AI-native OS value proposition
▌
▌### Decision 5: Observability Overhead
▌**Options:**
▌- A) Always-on comprehensive tracing
▌- B) Sampling-based with on-demand detail
▌- C) Minimal metrics only
▌
▌**Recommendation: B (Sampling-based)**
▌- **Pros**: Low overhead normally, full detail when needed
▌- **Cons**: May miss rare events, complexity in sampling logic
▌- **Rationale**: Balances production performance with debuggability
▌
▌## Conclusion
▌
▌This blueprint provides a concrete path from your current kernel to a research-grade AI-native OS. The staged approach
▌ensures measurable progress while maintaining CI stability. Key success factors:
▌
▌1. **Start with static graphs** for predictability, evolve to dynamic later
▌2. **Implement capabilities early** to avoid security retrofit
▌3. **Use CBS-EDF scheduling** for proven real-time guarantees
▌4. **Focus on zero-copy paths** for tensor operations
▌5. **Build observability in** from the start
▌
▌The 20-week timeline is aggressive but achievable with focused execution. Each milestone produces publishable results,
▌building toward a compelling SOSP/OSDI submission demonstrating the first purpose-built AI-native operating system.
▌

> Strong plan. Here’s my expert layer: decisions, corrections, and concrete next steps that unify the three consultations into
  one coherent, buildable path.
  
  What We Adopt
  
  - Dataflow-first: Graph/Operator/Port/Channel/Tensor as first-class kernel objects.
  - Capabilities-only security: model-centric tokens; signed model packages; measured load.
  - Determinism: CBS+EDF hybrid with admission control; static schedules for the deterministic subset.
  - Observability: operator-scoped tracepoints + PMU attribution; stable JSON schema.
  - SSI: consensus-free data plane; minimal control plane later; backpressure across nodes.
  
  Key Refinements (why and how)
  
  - Graph execution model:
      - Adopt static schedules for deterministic graphs; best-effort graphs may remain dynamic, but still graph-based.
      - Make “graph” the unit of isolation: memory pools, CPU reservations, and operator quotas live under Graph.
  - Zero-copy tensors:
      - Use page-backed, cache-line aligned pools; per-graph arenas for predictability.
      - Versioning = bump-on-write only at explicit mutation boundaries; keep “read sharing” cheap via refcounts.
      - Expose a single fast path: SPSC queue of Tensor handles, with optional small control messages (metadata deltas).
  - Channels and backpressure:
      - Phase 1: SPSC lock-free rings only (fast, analyzable). Push MPMC to Phase 2/3 when we need it.
      - Backpressure policy: fixed high/low watermarks; metrics for depth, stalls, drops. Keep policy simple and measurable.
  - Deterministic scheduling:
      - Deterministic graphs must be pre-admitted with WCET/period/deadline; no dynamic allocation inside operators.
      - CBS server per deterministic graph isolates bandwidth; EDF inside each CBS queue for operator order.
      - Timer discipline: event-driven, not tick-heavy; arm timer per deadline, avoid periodic jitter.
  - Capability model:
      - Cap = 64-bit id + sealed tag in kernel table; no crypto per check in the fast path.
      - Put crypto only on model load (hash+signature) and record a measurement log for later attestation.
  - Observability:
      - Always-on, low-overhead ring buffer for tracepoints; “sampling window” toggle for heavy events.
      - Schema version every time we add a field; keep operator_id, graph_id, ts, cpu, type in a stable header.
      - PMU attribution: fixed small set of counters (cycles, instructions, L1D miss, branch miss); avoid reprogramming
  thrash.
  - SSI prototype:
      - Start without Raft. Phase 3a = manual placement + heartbeats + epoch numbers. Phase 3b adds a tiny leader + replicated
  placement log.
      - RemoteChannel: reliable, in-order stream with credit-based flow control. Sequence numbers + acks; batch small tensors.
  
  Phase 1 Additions (4–6 weeks)
  
  - Kernel objects and APIs:
      - GraphCreate, OperatorAdd(fn_ptr, ports), ChannelCreate(capacity), GraphStart.
      - Memory: per-graph slab/arena; Tensor header aligned 64B; zero-copy handles only.
  - Scheduler:
      - Static topological order; run-to-completion; SPSC channels; backpressure via watermarks.
  - Metrics and tracing:
      - METRIC op_start/op_end, channel_depth, zero_copy_count, scheduler_cycle_us.
      - JSON: schema v1 with graph/operator sections; include percentile blocks for op latency.
  - DoD:
      - Demo “Graph OS” with 3–5 operators (e.g., preprocess → conv → pool → post) and measured end-to-end p95 improvement vs.
  a process/thread baseline.
  
  Phase 2 Additions (6–8 weeks)
  
  - Deterministic mode:
      - CBS+EDF queue per deterministic graph; admission control (Σ WCET/period <= bound).
      - Invariants: no alloc in op, bounded loops, no indefinite blocking; kernel enforces.
  - Model capabilities:
      - Signed package (SHA-256 + Ed25519); measurement log; capabilities for LOAD/RUN/INSPECT.
      - Simple secure model “store” interface (opaque handle, version id) with rollback protection flag.
  - Metrics:
      - det_miss_count, det_jitter_ns, model_load_ok/fail, admission_reject_count.
  - DoD:
      - Deterministic inference demo with reproducible p99 jitter bound and a failing unsigned model load test.
  
  Phase 3 Additions (8–10 weeks)
  
  - Transport:
      - Virtio-net framed messages (len|type|seq|flags|crc|payload); send credits; retry on timeout; batch frames.
  - Placement:
      - Manual placement map; kernel inserts RemoteChannels; backpressure crosses nodes.
  - Fault tolerance:
      - Heartbeats; epoch bump + teardown on failure; user-space restarts graph.
  - Metrics:
      - remote_latency_p95_us, retry_rate, placement_time_ms, node_failures.
  - DoD:
      - 2-node split graph with throughput scaling and graceful degradation under induced node failure.
  
  Validation and CI guardrails
  
  - Reproducibility: fixed seeds, fixed config snapshot; 100-run distributions; QEMU thresholds separate from hardware.
  - Acceptance thresholds:
      - P1: zero-copy speedup vs. copy (>2x for 64KB+ tensors); op p95 latency tracked.
      - P2: admission rejects overload; jitter p99 within bound; no dynamic allocs detected in deterministic ops.
      - P3: remote link p95 latency target (<1 ms in QEMU), retry rate <1%, scaling >1.5x vs single node for pipelined graphs.
  
  Gaps to close (pragmatic tweaks)
  
  - Static vs dynamic: Keep deterministic graphs static for now; dynamic placement waits for Phase 3b.
  - Raft scope: Defer Raft until after manual placement + epoch works. Don’t put Raft in the data plane.
  - “True zero-copy” over net: On QEMU/virtio, it’s zero-copy at the API boundary, not wire-level. Be explicit and measure
  copies.
  - Cryptography footprint: Pick one signature scheme (Ed25519) and one hash (SHA-256) to minimize code size; do verification
  in a dedicated, measured path.
  
  Extra references worth borrowing
  
  - Barrelfish (multikernel) — split mechanism/policy, message-passing OS. Takeaway: keep per-core, per-node independence;
  communicate explicitly. https://www.barrelfish.org
  - TFRT (TensorFlow Runtime) — static graph executor/runtime. Takeaway: separate compile vs run; small runtime ops. https://
  github.com/tensorflow/runtime
  - Linux SCHED_DEADLINE docs and Lelli et al. — EDF with admission control. Takeaway: utilization checks; runtime/deadline
  semantics. https://lwn.net/Articles/636631/
  - seL4 object model — minimal capability kernel. Takeaway: tiny TCB and capability discipline. https://sel4.systems
  - ARM ARM (A-profile) memory model and PMU — authoritative details for barriers/counters. Takeaway: use Acquire/Release;
  avoid over-fencing. https://developer.arm.com/documentation
  
  Immediate next actions (this week)
  
  - Skeleton modules: kernel::graph, kernel::channel::spsc, kernel::tensor::pool, kernel::cap::table.
  - Minimal syscalls or in-kernel APIs for Graph/Operator/Channel create/start.
  - Ring-buffer tracing with schema v1 and 3–5 core METRICs wired into the runner.
  - “Sobel chain” demo graph and baseline comparison path in the test runner.
  
  If you want, I can draft the initial kernel modules (stubs + metric hooks) and update the test runner schema to v1 so you
  can start Phase 1 implementation with clear compile targets and CI checks.

    196   +    current_util + (wcet as f64 / period as f64) <= 1.0
    197   +}
    198   +```
    199   +
    200   +## References (Selected, With Takeaways)
    201   +
    202   +- seL4 (SOSP 2009): Minimal capability kernel; keep TCB tiny; capability discipline throughout.
    203   +- Linux SCHED_DEADLINE (Lelli et al.): EDF + admission control; utilization bounds and timer discipline.
    204   +- Abeni & Buttazzo CBS (RTSS 1998): Bandwidth servers to isolate mixed workloads.
    205   +- TensorFlow TFRT: Static graph runtime; separate compile vs run; small, efficient ops.
    206   +- Barrelfish: Multikernel message‑passing; separate mechanism from policy; per‑core independence.
    207   +- Google Dapper: Tracing principles; low overhead, context propagation.
    208   +- ARM ARM + PMU Docs: Barriers, memory model, counter programming; avoid over‑fencing; attribute wisely.
    209   +

    1     +//! Lock-free Single-Producer Single-Consumer ring buffer.
    2     +//! Suitable for zero-copy handle passing in Phase 1.
    3     +
    4     +use core::mem::MaybeUninit;
    5     +use core::sync::atomic::{AtomicUsize, Ordering};
    6     +
    7     +pub struct Spsc<T: Copy, const N: usize> {
    8     +    buf: [MaybeUninit<T>; N],
    9     +    head: AtomicUsize,
    10    +    tail: AtomicUsize,
    11    +}
    12    +
    13    +impl<T: Copy, const N: usize> Spsc<T, N> {
    14    +    pub const fn new() -> Self {
    15    +        // const-init workaround: MaybeUninit::uninit_array not const-stable in core for all versions
    16    +        Self {
    17    +            buf: unsafe { MaybeUninit::<[MaybeUninit<T>; N]>::uninit().assume_init() },
    18    +            head: AtomicUsize::new(0),
    19    +            tail: AtomicUsize::new(0),
    20    +        }
    21    +    }
    22    +
    23    +    #[inline(always)]
    24    +    pub fn capacity(&self) -> usize { N }
    25    +
    26    +    #[inline(always)]
    27    +    pub fn try_enqueue(&self, v: T) -> Result<(), T> {
    28    +        let tail = self.tail.load(Ordering::Relaxed);
    29    +        let head = self.head.load(Ordering::Acquire);
    30    +        let next = (tail + 1) % N;
    31    +        if next == head { return Err(v); }
    32    +        unsafe { (*self.buf.get_unchecked(tail).as_ptr()) = v; }
    33    +        self.tail.store(next, Ordering::Release);
    34    +        Ok(())
    35    +    }
    36    +
    37    +    #[inline(always)]
    38    +    pub fn try_dequeue(&self) -> Option<T> {
    39    +        let head = self.head.load(Ordering::Relaxed);
    40    +        let tail = self.tail.load(Ordering::Acquire);
    41    +        if head == tail { return None; }
    42    +        let v = unsafe { (*self.buf.get_unchecked(head).as_ptr()) };
    43    +        self.head.store((head + 1) % N, Ordering::Release);
    44    +        Some(v)
    45    +    }
    46    +}
    47    +

> I’ve scaffolded Phase 1 and wired a minimal demo into the kernel bring‑up.
  
  What I Implemented
  
  - Trace utilities: crates/kernel/src/trace.rs
      - metric_kv(name, value) and trace(tag) for low‑overhead METRIC/TRACE lines.
  - Capabilities (stub): crates/kernel/src/cap.rs
      - CapId, CapRights, Capability, and a fast check() predicate. Keeps kernel surface minimal for now.
  - Tensors (minimal): crates/kernel/src/tensor/mod.rs
      - TensorHeader, TensorHandle, and a simple TensorAlloc alloc/dealloc using the global allocator (arenas arrive later).
  - Channels (SPSC ring): crates/kernel/src/channel/spsc.rs
      - Lock‑free single‑producer/single‑consumer ring buffer with acquire/release ordering and zero‑copy handle passing.
  - Graph scaffolding + demo: crates/kernel/src/graph.rs
      - Tiny two‑operator “pipeline” that uses the SPSC ring to move items and measures total cycles (cntvct) → ns conversion.
      - Emits METRICs:
      - `METRIC graph_demo_total_ns=<ns>`
      - `METRIC graph_demo_items=<n>`
      - `METRIC graph_demo_avg_ns_per_item=<ns>`
  - Bring‑up integration: crates/kernel/src/main.rs
      - After heap tests, runs a “GRAPH: DEMO” pass that builds the pipeline and emits the metrics.
  
  Build Status
  
  - cargo check -p sis_kernel passes (no warnings).
  - Code compiles on host (non‑AArch64) via cfg‑gated timer/PMU reads; AArch64 paths use CNTVCT/CNTFRQ.
  
  How to See It
  
  - On AArch64/QEMU bring‑up (BRINGUP=1 ./scripts/uefi_run.sh), after heap tests you’ll see:
      - GRAPH: DEMO
      - METRIC lines for graph_demo_*
      - GRAPH: DEMO DONE
  
  Why This Matters (Phase 1 readiness)
  
  - Establishes the core primitives: Graph, Operator, Channel (SPSC), Tensor (handle), and METRIC emission.
  - Provides a clean place to add:
      - Operator start/end tracepoints and PMU attribution.
      - Per‑graph arenas and zero‑copy tensor semantics.
      - Deterministic scheduler mode and capability checks later.
  
  Proposed Next Steps
  
  - Phase 1 completion
      - Add operator tracepoints: op_start/op_end, channel_depth, zero_copy_count.
      - Introduce per‑graph memory arenas (cache‑aligned, page‑backed) and version bump on mutation.
      - Expand Graph API (create/start/add operator/channel) + simple priority scheduler loop.
      - Update testing runner to parse graph_demo_* and prepare schema v1 keys.
  - Phase 2 prep
      - CBS+EDF deterministic mode stubs (admission control structure, timer discipline).
      - Capability gates on Channel WRITE/Graph RUN; model loader hooks (signed package entry point).

  first?

    56    +}
    57    +
    58    +impl<const N: usize> BumpArena<N> {
    59    +    pub const fn new() -> Self { Self { buf: Aligned([0; N]), off: 0 } }
    60    +
    61    +    #[inline(always)]
    62    +    pub fn remaining(&self) -> usize { N.saturating_sub(self.off) }
    63    +

    65    +    pub fn alloc(&mut self, size: usize, align: usize) -> Option<TensorHandle> {
    66    +        let base = self.buf.0.as_ptr() as usize;
    67    +        let mut cur = base + self.off;
    68    +        let aligned = (cur + (align - 1)) & !(align - 1);
    69    +        let end = aligned.checked_add(size)?;
    70    +        if end > base + N { return None; }
    71    +        self.off = end - base;
    72    +        Some(TensorHandle { ptr: aligned as *mut u8, len: size })
    73    +    }

      - Producer allocates 64‑byte buffers from a per‑graph BumpArena and enqueues TensorHandle when the channel isn’t full.
      - Consumer dequeues TensorHandle and increments a handle-specific counter.
      - Emitted new METRIC: zero_copy_handle_count (in addition to zero_copy_count).
  - Operator tracing (kernel):
      - Added op_start(id) and op_end_ns(id, ns) tracepoints around operator runs (already added earlier).
      - Maintains op_a_runs, op_b_runs, op_a_total_ns, op_b_total_ns.
  - Arena metric (kernel):
      - Continues to emit arena_remaining_bytes for bump arena sanity.
  - Channel helpers (kernel):
      - depth(), is_full(), is_empty() support backpressure and metrics.
  - Testing ingestion (runner):
      - Parser now captures zero_copy_handle_count and includes it in metrics_dump.json.

  - cargo check -p sis-testing passes.

> Implemented the minimal Graph API and refactored the demo to use it, plus finished the zero-copy handle path.
  
  What’s in place now
  
  - Graph API (kernel)
      - GraphApi::create(): new graph.
      - add_channel(ChannelSpec { capacity }) -> usize: creates an SPSC<TensorHandle, 64> channel.
      - add_operator(OperatorSpec { id, func, in_ch, out_ch, priority }) -> usize: records a single-in/single-out operator
  binding.
      - is_runnable(op_idx) -> bool: true when input not empty (if any) and output not full (if any).
      - channel(idx) -> &Spsc<TensorHandle, 64>: read/write access for scheduling code.
      - Internals: lightweight OpNode with in/out channel mapping and priority fields (kept for future ordering).
  - Graph demo refactor (kernel)
      - GraphDemo now builds a GraphApi with two channels and two operators (A: out→ch_ab; B: in←ch_ab, out→ch_bc).
      - Scheduling loop uses the Graph API:
      - Checks `is_runnable` and runs in static priority order (A then B).
      - Producer: allocates `TensorHandle` from `BumpArena` (64B aligned) and enqueues into `ch_ab`.
      - Consumer: dequeues from `ch_ab`, forwards to `ch_bc`, and increments counters.
  - Operator tracepoints: emits [TRACE] op_start and [TRACE] op_end ... ns= around each activation.
  - Metrics emitted:
      - `graph_demo_total_ns`, `graph_demo_items`, `graph_demo_avg_ns_per_item`
      - `channel_ab_depth_max`, `zero_copy_count`, `zero_copy_handle_count`
      - `op_a_runs`, `op_b_runs`, `op_a_total_ns`, `op_b_total_ns`
      - `arena_remaining_bytes`
  - Testing parser (runner)
      - Ingests zero_copy_handle_count along with the earlier graph demo and operator fields and writes them to
  metrics_dump.json.
  
  Build status
  
  - cargo check -p sis_kernel --features strict passes.
  - cargo check -p sis-testing passes.
  
  Next logical steps
  
  - Priority: Add optional PMU attribution per operator behind a feature flag (cycles + one cache event), and summarize as
  METRICs.
  - Add a small static-priority runnable loop inside GraphApi (e.g., run_steps(n)) and have GraphDemo call it, reducing demo
  code.
  - Start wiring real operator functions to use OperatorCtx (enqueue/dequeue via ctx), moving logic out of the demo loop.
